I’ve just finished implementing the core engine modules: world building, physics, player rendering, sound synthesis, and the main game client. The user’s last message was “Now the studio editor — collaborative 3D place editor.” They’re expecting the next piece of the codebase to be the studio/editor front‑end that ties into the engine I’ve already built.

First, I should verify what parts of the project are still missing. The directory structure under `public/js` currently contains:
- `api.js` (network API wrapper)
- `avatar2d.js` (2D avatar drawing)
- `engine/` with `world.js`, `physics.js`, `player.js`, `sfx.js`, `game.js`
- No `studio/` folder yet.

The studio editor will need to import utilities from the engine (scene setup, part mesh creation) and from the API (state handling, WebSocket opening, toast notifications). I recall that `world.js` exports `setupScene`, `World`, and also a helper `createPartMesh` that I added earlier for rendering parts. Let me double‑check that `createPartMesh` exists – yes, in `world.js` I defined a function that returns a Mesh for a given part definition, used by both the game client and should be reusable for the editor.

Given the pattern of the other modules, each file starts with a comment header describing its purpose, then imports, then constants, then the main class with a constructor that builds the DOM, sets up the scene, connects networking, binds input, and runs an animation loop. The style of the code should match the rest of the project: use ES6 modules, three.js, and the shared `state`, `openWS`, `esc`, `toast` utilities.

I need to decide on the exact filename and path. The user said “studio editor” – following the existing naming convention, it should live under `public/js/studio/` and be called `studio.js`. That matches the pattern `engine/*.js`. I’ll create that file.

Now I need to flesh out the content. I’ll start with a comment header:

```js
// Studio: collaborative place editor. Fly camera, part placement on a grid,
...
```

Next imports: three.js, plus `setupScene`, `World`, and `createPartMesh` from the engine’s `world.js`. Also import `state`, `openWS`, `esc`, `toast` from `../api.js` (relative path from studio folder). That mirrors how `game.js` imports from `../api.js`.

Then I need to define constants for part definitions (type, label, color, size). I can reuse the same list that the engine uses for part types, but include a broader palette for the editor UI. I’ll create `PART_DEFS` array with objects for each part type (block, spawn, checkpoint, kill, coin, goal, bounce, speed, water, deco, mover, tele). The sizes should match the default sizes used elsewhere.

Also define `COLOR_PALETTE` (a set of colors for the color picker) and arrays for `MODES` and `GENRES` for the game config panel.

Now the `Studio` class. Its constructor will accept `(root, gameId, onExit)`, similar to `GameClient`. Inside, store parameters, initialize tool state (`select` by default), placeType, selection ID, editors map, key state, camera position/yaw/pitch, alive flag, undo stack.

Then call `_buildDOM()` to construct the UI. I’ll design a top bar with a title, game name placeholder, tool buttons (select, place, delete), a spacer, an editors list, test and exit buttons. Below that, a main area with a canvas for three.js and a side panel containing sections for parts palette, properties, game config, and team chat. The DOM string should be inserted via `innerHTML`. After that, cache references to the canvas, side elements, etc.

In `_buildDOM`, after creating the palette buttons, I need to set up click handlers to change `placeType` and call `setTool('place')`. Also bind the top‑bar tool buttons via their `data-tool` attributes, and hook up exit and test buttons. The chat input should send a `chat` message on Enter.

Next, after building the DOM, set up the three.js scene using `setupScene(this.canvas)`, store renderer, scene, camera, resize function. Create a `World` instance with the scene.

Add grid helper, selection box helper (initially invisible). Initialize raycaster and a ground plane for placement.

Then call `_connect()` to open a WebSocket via `openWS()`. On open, send a `studio` join message with the `gameId`. Set up `onmessage` to parse JSON and forward to `_handle`.

In `_handle`, implement cases for `error`, `sjoined` (initial data: selfId, meta, config, ownership, world parts, existing editors), `sjoin` (new editor joins), `sleave` (editor leaves), `sel` (remote selection), `op` (remote operation), `opok` (server acknowledgment for adds), and `chat`. For each, update UI, world, editors map, etc. Follow the patterns used in `game.js` for similar messages.

Implement `_addEditor`, `_renderEditors`, `_updateRemoteHighlight` (draw a Box3Helper around a selected part for a remote user), and `_applyRemoteOp` to handle add/update/delete/meta operations from other collaborators, updating the world and UI accordingly.

Next, define local operation helpers `_opAdd`, `_opUpdate`, `_opDel`, and `_undo` that modify the local world, send the op to the server, and push undo entries.

Selection handling: `_select(partId)` sends a `sel` message, updates selection box visibility, and calls `_renderProps(part)`. `_renderProps` builds a properties UI with inputs for position, size, color swatches, and extra fields for special part types (mover, tele, checkpoint). It attaches change listeners that call `_opUpdate` and re‑select to refresh.

Config panel: `_renderConfig` builds UI for game metadata and config (name, description, genre, mode, max players, gravity, walk speed, jump power, respawn time, public checkbox). Save button gathers values and sends a `meta` op, then shows a toast.

Input binding: `_bindInput` registers global keydown/up listeners, handling tool shortcuts (1,2,3), delete/backspace, undo (Ctrl/Cmd+Z), duplicate (Ctrl/Cmd+D). Also sets up mouse events on the canvas: mousedown for look drag (right button) or start dragging selected part (left button with select tool), mouseup for clicks (select, delete, place), mousemove for camera rotation, part dragging, or ghost placement, contextmenu prevention, wheel for dolly.

Implement helper methods `_ndc`, `_pickPart`, `_rayToPlane`, `_updateGhost`. `_updateGhost` creates or updates a semi‑transparent mesh representing the part being placed, snapping to the grid or on top of existing parts.

Loop: `_loop` runs requestAnimationFrame, computes delta time, calls resize, updates camera position based on WASD and other keys, updates world tick, updates selection box position if needed, renders.

Finally, `exit(to)` cleans up: set alive false, cancel animation, remove event listeners, close WS, dispose renderer, and call `onExit`.

All of this mirrors the architecture of the rest of the codebase and provides the collaborative editing features the user requested. I’ve now composed the complete source for `studio.js` with all necessary imports, constants, class definition, and methods.
